subjects.note: Rail lines run into factories and yards — the industrial city, mostly gone by 1930.
A lot split in two, or a building divided into flats that sell separately.
How affordable housing is paid for, in the years since the 1980s.
Sewers laid, broken, replaced — and occasionally sinking with the ground.
Steps, planters, ramps and parklets standing on public sidewalk.

summary: For its first eighty years this was a rail yard and a tidal channel, and the record is mostly track. The Board handed out spur tracks one at a time — to the Monadnock Brick Company on Sixteenth Street in 1907, to the Pacific Oil and Lead Works off King Street the same year, to the Felton Company on Second Street in 1909, to Crane Company on Second Street in 1926 — and in 1926 it printed a list of every spur track permit granted since 1916. It bridged the Channel at Third Street with a bascule bridge in 1930, $320,000 out of a bond fund, the State Harbor Commissioners paying half. It had already put a temporary sewage pumping station on Fourth Street near Berry in 1907, and in 1912 it bought the incinerator — the Sanitary Reduction Works — for $400,000. It made the railroad pay for the street as well: in 1919 it directed the Southern Pacific to grade, curb and pave Townsend Street between Fourth and Eighth, and the company agreed to begin by April of the following year. In 1959 a printing firm was allowed to park on the Berry Street sidewalk. Then the whole place was replanned. A ground lease for a ballpark was signed in 1997 and a redevelopment plan for Mission Bay South adopted in 1998; in 2000 the Board asked that the south side of King Street be renamed 24 Willie Mays Plaza. What followed was a neighbourhood assembled out of paperwork: parts of Fourth Street vacated, the old easements under Hubbell Street given up, parks dedicated and named one by one, and condominium buildings of 99, 111, 224, 263 and 329 units approved between 2006 and 2012 with housing bonds behind many of them. Two survivors from before got their names written down — the Dunham, Carrigan & Hayden Building at 2 Henry Adams Street in 2018, and the Takahashi Trading Company at 200 Rhode Island Street in 2022.
